It is well known as a way of managing tax missteps and risk during mergers and acquisitions and company reorganizations or to insure alternative energy tax credit. But tax liability insurance is less familiar and equally useful in asset management where it can be deployed to vastly speed up closing a fund for a minimal cost.
When a fund has an uncertain lifespan
Alternative investment funds often have a fixed lifespan. They spend the first few years buying illiquid assets and then spend the remaining years selling them off.
However, fund liabilities can have a long, uncertain lifespan, making their wind-down difficult and slow. Contingent tax liabilities can have a long tail of six or more years due to statutes of limitations in certain US jurisdictions.
Hedge funds can often give investors their money back regularly because they hold assets that are easy to sell based on investor demand for capital. But private equity funds, credit funds, infrastructure funds and real estate funds generally consist of illiquid assets that need to be sold opportunistically and generally can’t provide investors with full liquidity.
As a result, private equity fund managers will frequently advertise an expected investment period and expected fund lifespan – without making any assurances. But investors can be reluctant to invest without an indication of when they’ll see a return on their money.
Fund managers earn performance bonuses (carried interest) based on how quickly they return cash to investors. To hit these targets and wrap up an aging fund, managers sometimes sell their remaining assets to a new, secondary fund, often called a continuation fund backed by a different group of investors or a subset of the original investors.
However, fund managers struggle to control how long a fund’s financial obligations last, and buyers who take over existing funds usually don’t want to inherit old debts and risks. In the investment world, tax liabilities are especially problematic because they can linger for a very long time.
Tax liabilities, a long-tail risk
Certain tax liabilities can, of course, be eliminated by paying the appropriate tax authority. But contingent tax risks relating to uncertain positions taken by the fund can have a significantly longer tail.
In the US, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) generally has three years to audit a tax return, but this extends to six years if you substantially underreport your income. Ongoing disputes can drag on much longer if the IRS asks for more time to finish an audit or there are court delays. This is when tax insurance can be an alternative asset manager’s best friend.
The solution: tax insurance
Tax insurance is a rapidly growing tool for managing tax risk but is particularly useful for alternative asset managers, who can use it to close down funds sooner without having to worry about investor holdbacks or clawbacks.
It shifts the financial risk of a tax dispute from a company, funds or investors to an insurer. Tax insurance generally covers potential losses for additional taxes, interest, penalties, and defense costs.
Unlike slow IRS private letter rulings, tax insurance can be bought in just a few weeks to quickly protect your tax position. The American Property Casualty Insurance Association is one of eight organizations pushing federal lawmakers to rethink and fine tune legislation regarding consumer choice when it comes to vehicle repair.
The matter, they said, is important because current limitations on just how and where vehicles are fixed has increased the cost of repairs because parts in some cases are limited to more expensive original equipment manufacturer (OEM) options, and access to vehicle-generated diagnostics, data, and software is restricted – especially when it comes to modern vehicles.
A federal standard is needed to ensure consumers have the right to choose who repairs their vehicles and what parts are used.
“According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, over the last five years in the absence of a federal right to repair, vehicle repair costs increased over 40%,” said the groups signing the letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Along with the APCIA, others include the Auto Care Association, CAR Coalition, MEMA Aftermarket Suppliers, Commercial Vehicle Solutions Network, National Federation of Independent Business, National Independent Automobile Dealers Association, and Preventative Automotive Maintenance Association.
They said they’d like to see more provisions within the Right to Equitable and Professional Auto Industry Repair (REPAIR) Act (HR 1566) included in any legislation. Provisions of the REPAIR Act were included earlier this year within another piece of legislation, the Motor Vehicle Modernization Act of 2026 (HR 7389), passed by a House committee. However, REPAIR Act sponsor Neal Dunn (R-Fla.) has said the legislation passed “does not fully reflect the original REPAIR Act and fails to protect consumers, independent repair shops, and aftermarket manufacturers.”
The organizations signing the letter to House leaders apparently agree. The MVMA Act included “repair provisions based largely on limited voluntary memoranda of understanding developed more than a decade ago. These agreements fail to meet automotive repair marketplace needs in 2026,” they said.
“Recent developments underscore why voluntary industry policies are not enough,” the groups continued, adding that General Motors recently released its position that it “strictly prohibits” use of non-OEM parts for repair.
“This guidance effectively restricts consumer choice and forces the use of more expensive OEM parts,” the groups said. “GM’s position statement is illustrative of a broader trend: Several other automakers, including Ford, Honda, and Nissan, have rolled out similar restrictions.
“Consumers should continue to have a choice of lawful, safe, and equivalent repair options.”

Nvidia Corp. is being investigated by California officials to determine whether any of its actions resulted in advanced chips or confidential information being improperly obtained by China.
The state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, said in a statement Thursday that his office is also looking into whether the company misled investors about the situation. Nvidia was sent a subpoena seeking information to determine if the company violated the state’s corporate security law, he said.
Related: Nvidia Scandal Raises New Concerns About Scale of Chinese Spying
Jensen Huang’s disclosure last week of an extramarital affair plunged Nvidia into an unprecedented crisis, fueling a sharp selloff in the company’s shares and resulting in his ouster as chief executive officer. His disclosure also led to potential national security concerns following reports that he had a relationship with Alice Huang and that US officials suspected her of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
Also on Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released confidential information showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies this year as of May, including to some that were later added to a Pentagon list of businesses accused of aiding China’s military.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”
Santa Clara, California-based Nvidia did not respond to a message seeking comment.
Nvidia is the world’s largest chipmaker and was, until recently, the world’s most valuable publicly-traded company. Under Huang’s leadership its products became central to the massive build out in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
In a Bloomberg Television interview on Tuesday, Bonta described the situation as “very possibly” something his office could examine. He added that his course of action would be determined by whether any California laws could have been broken, which would establish jurisdiction for his office.
Beijing has denied that it attempted to spy on Jensen Huang, who is not related to Alice Huang. On Tuesday, Huang expressed a willingness to return to the helm although the board isn’t currently considering such an idea, Bloomberg News reported.
Bonta, a Democrat who won reelection earlier this month, has been scrutinizing Big Tech more broadly, including by filing a lawsuit against OpenAI for allegedly violating the state’s unfair competition law by unsafely developing its AI products.

US Senate panel grills Trump cyber director about outages making people ‘jittery’
The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on April 18, 2024. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — Members of the U.S. Senate Homeland Security committee Thursday questioned the potential new head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency about nationwide security disruptions that members of Congress said have left the American public on edge.
Democrats also accused the Trump administration of trying to quickly confirm that nominee and others during the lame-duck session of Congress, before Democrats gain majority control of the Senate in January. Democrats are set to come in with 56 seats.
Oklahoma Republican James Lankford, who is running to serve as the top GOP senator on the committee in the next Congress, defended President Donald Trump’s decision to make the nominations now.
“The White House seemed to have followed the letter of the law,” Lankford said. “I’m not completely sure they followed the entire spirit of the law, but they have actually gone through the process that needs to be done to be able to put the nominees forward, to be able to have the input.”
Trump nominated Michael LoSapio to be Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, housed within the Department of Homeland Security. The agency handles election security and oversees protection of federal infrastructure from cyber attacks.
Senators also questioned at length a nominee who has generated opposition among Democrats, Eric M. Ueland, whom Trump has tapped to be comptroller general of the U.S. Government Accountability Office, the top federal government watchdog agency.
Scary tech outages
Widespread technology outages have occurred for days across the United States, including tens of thousands of canceled flights, transaction problems at major banks and shut-down email services at the National Security Agency.
Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a former national security federal government worker, grilled LoSapio about nationwide cyber outages.
“American citizens are jittery,” she said.
She raised concerns about the Trump administration’s decision to eliminate more than 1,000 positions at CISA. She asked LoSapio if he agreed with that decision and if he thinks CISA needs more funding.
LoSapio said he couldn’t comment “on the current state of CISA,” because he was coming in from the private sector. LoSapio is Palantir Technology Inc.’s chief information security officer.
LoSapio added that once he evaluates the agency, if he feels CISA needs more funding, he would ask Congress.
“I’m going to get involved and understand where the gaps are, and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis,” he said.
Slotkin said she was not satisfied with his answer.
“At the end of the day, every American knows that cyberattacks are going up, that the risks are going up,” she said. “You should be able to say clearly, ‘There’s increasing threat, therefore, we need increasing resources to deal with it.’”
Connecticut Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked LoSapio about who won the 2020 presidential election, because CISA deals with election security. Trump has falsely claimed that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him, and galvanized a mob of his supporters to stop the certification of the election by storming the U.S. Capitol.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said.

Years of drawing down reserves have left lawmakers facing difficult choices over funding for public schools, Medicaid and other state services
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe delivering his 2025 budget message to lawmakers. Kehoe will present a new budget in January and must find $3 billion to cover the difference between likely revenue and requested spending (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).
Missouri faces a gap of almost $3 billion between the cost of keeping state government agencies open in the coming fiscal year and available tax revenue, according to a review of department budget requests.
That gap is equivalent to nearly one-fifth of the requested spending from the state’s general revenue fund, which relies primarily on income and sales taxes to pay for public schools, healthcare, prisons and other programs.
For five years, the state has appropriated more general revenue than it received. Over that period, a fund balance that stood at $5.7 billion on June 30, 2023, is expected, under the most recent official estimate, to be about $265 million by June 30, 2027.

Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin, a Shelbina Republican, will lead Missouri’s Department of Elementary and Secondary Education as interim commissioner of education beginning Dec. 1.
The State Board of Education voted 6-1 to appoint O’Laughlin in a closed meeting Friday morning. It will continue its search for a permanent commissioner, aiming to hire a permanent commissioner by June.
“I recognize that this is an interim role, and my responsibility is to provide steady leadership while the board continues its search for a permanent commissioner,” O’Laughlin told The Independent Friday afternoon. “I have told the board I will not be vying for that position. But that doesn’t mean we should stand still.”
The board has “important work underway to improve accountability, establish clear goals and focus on student achievement,” she said. The department is currently working on an A-F grading system for public schools requested by Gov. Mike Kehoe, drawing criticism from educators who fear schools’ reputation will be impacted by a scoring system they see as flawed.
“I am ready to roll up my sleeves and get to work,” O’Laughlin said. “Our kids deserve nothing less.”
She will replace Lisa Sireno, who has served as interim commissioner since Oct. 21 following the resignation of Stacey Preis.
Missouri state education board selects interim commissioner amid leadership shakeup
The announcement came after months of rumors that O’Laughlin was being eyed for the position. As word circulated more widely in the past month, the state board’s inbox filled with angry emails and questions about her qualifications.
Wheaton school Superintendent Alyssa Kennedy was among those who opposed O’Laughlin’s possible appointment, sharing her letter to the board in a Facebook post.
“I respectfully urge the Board not to make this appointment based on political alignment or a predetermined outcome,” she wrote. “If the Board is considering Senator O’Laughlin, I urge you to carefully examine whether her experience and policy positions align with the responsibilities and public mission of this office.”
State law requires the commissioner to “possess an educational attainment and breadth of experience in the administration of public education.”
O’Laughlin’s Senate biography says she has experience “as a school bus driver, an administrator at a local Christian school and as a member of her local school board.” The Independent could not find record of her work in these positions.

Roberta Groner had what she calls “a rocky road” for the year leading up to the New York City Marathon on November 1.
In her previous three attempts at the marathon, during which she had hoped to run an Olympic Marathon Trials qualifying time (2:37), she had racked up three DNFs in a row.
She was in great shape for the Valencia Marathon in December 2025, having just run 1:12:21 for the half marathon, and she thought she might be in shape to better her lifetime PR in the marathon, which is 2:29:09, from 2019, when she was 41. Her conservative goal was getting the Trials time.
But a warm day in Spain—about 75 degrees—and a brain lock about translating kilometers into miles caused her to step off the course late in the race. Her coach, Devon Martin, of the Central Park Track Club, still rues that one. “She had no idea she had seven minutes to spare at mile 18,” Martin said.
Two weeks later, Groner hopped in the Marathon Project in Arizona. Martin had tried to convince her not to. Sure enough, her legs hadn’t recovered from the hard miles in Valencia, and she dropped out there, too.
Then came Grandma’s Marathon in June in Duluth, Minnesota. Groner felt off. She later realized that her body was adjusting to starting hormone replacement therapy for perimenopause symptoms. Another DNF.
By the time she got to New York City, her hometown race, Groner—a former nurse who is now a full-time coach with Central Park Track Club—was uncharacteristically a basket case.
“I had to fight some mental demons, especially the week before,” she said. “My coach was probably like, ‘Oh, I can't handle her.’”
Groner ran with the elite women, always a small group in New York, which leaves those who can’t keep pace with the strange sensation of running a big-city marathon alone. She was well behind the leaders, running side-by-side with Steph Bruce for the first 17 miles, before Bruce fell back. Groner spent the next 9 miles with her eyes scanning the distance for any women she could pick off on the way to the finish.
She passed a handful of runners in the final stretch and finished 22nd in 2:35:55, her third Olympic Trials qualifier. She’ll be 50 when the race goes off in St. Louis. Dot McMahan of Michigan, who has qualified for her sixth trials, will be 51.
“I was able to race and compete, which was great,” Groner said. “And yeah, it wasn't my fastest New York, but I was really happy with the performance. Knowing that my faster days could be done, I still want to race really well. To be able to pass a few people at the end. I’ll give it an A.”
But are her fastest days really behind her? Groner doesn’t necessarily think so. And she’s not backing off her goals just because she’s in her late 40s.

When Cameron Balser arrived at New York City Hall at 11:45 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 20, 2026, he set a new speed record for the Trans America Run, a route stretching from San Francisco, California, on the West Coast, to New York City on the East Coast and covering 3,067 miles (4,935 kilometers).
He’d been running on the route, affectionately called the “TransAm,” for 41 days, 16 hours, and 45 minutes, and he was joined by a large crowd on the streets of New York City to celebrate his accomplishment.
When Balser left the San Francisco City Hall at 5:00 a.m. Pacific Daylight Time, on October 10, he was chasing Pete Kostelnick’s record from 2016. Kostelnick ran between the city halls in 42 days, 6 hours, and 30 minutes. With seemingly the tightest of margins for a run of this length, Balser broke Kostelnick’s time by 13 hours and 45 minutes.
He’d covered more than 140,000 feet of elevation gain while traversing across California, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Nebraska, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and finally New York, and averaged 73.61 miles per day. Running over mountains, through deserts and prairies, and everything in between, Basler’s consistency over all types of terrain was impressive, both with his efficient crew and his steady pace.
Across the Country
The 35-year-old Indiana native named his run “Breaking 42,” making his intentions to run farther than Kostelnick’s 72.56-mile daily average clear from the start. Winter weather delays in the Rockies complicated Balser’s plans early on, including a forced early stop due to rain that made a dirt road impassable for support-vehicle access and snow at the high point of his route, Cameron Pass, in Colorado.
With remarkable consistency, Balser broke his 15- to 16-hour days into five-mile segments, taking in around 800 calories at each crew stop to keep his energy levels up. He aimed to run every uphill stretch to finish each day’s mileage as efficiently as possible.
Once out of the Colorado mountains, Balser went on to surge across the prairies, cranking out 75-mile days through the flatter terrain of the Midwest and East Coast as he closed in on New York. Throughout the route, he was joined by friends and fans, and he kept a live tracker available for anyone who wanted to share miles with him.
Unlike a fixed trail fastest known time where the route is defined, the Trans America Run record is defined by its endpoints — the San Francisco City Hall and New York City Hall — and Balser’s crew spent months studying Kostelnick’s 2016 blueprint, even joking on social media that they were “sick and tired of studying [his] route/record.”
Prior record holder Kostelnick cheered Balser on throughout his attempt. A couple of days before Balser’s finish, he quipped on social media: “It’s always humbling to see a record you put so (damn) much into get broken, but I’ve learned it also requires genuine appreciation for the person willing to chase your ghost. To really recognize them, especially when they’ve done it the right way. San Francisco to NYC. Showing happiness over clicks. Give us more of that, Cameron.”
On the final night, Balser was joined by several dozen runners for the last 11 miles in from the George Washington Bridge. Most income investors trade growth for yield. This ETF lets you have both.
By Keith Speights –
Key Points
- The Goldman Sachs S&P 500 Core Premium Income ETF holds S&P 500 stocks and sells call options on 25% to 75% of the portfolio to generate income.
- It has paid an 8.3% distribution yield over the past year while delivering average annual returns of 20.4% since its 2023 launch.
- The ETF is best for income investors who want some growth.
Many income investors view the trade-off between high yields and growth potential as a necessary evil. They think having both is virtually impossible.
However, that doesn't have to be the case. The Goldman Sachs S&P 500 Core Premium Income ETF (GPIX -3.38%) offers both high yields and growth. This dividend ETF could be the passive income and growth engine that many investors didn't know existed.

What sets this ETF apart
Like several top S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) index funds, the Goldman Sachs S&P 500 Core Premium Income ETF provides exposure to the S&P 500. Its top holdings include the largest components of the S&P 500 index itself: Apple (AAPL -1.90%), Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%), Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%), Amazon (AMZN -4.10%), and Alphabet (GOOG -2.59%) (GOOGL -2.70%).
But this isn't an ordinary S&P 500 ETF. Two words in the fund's name hint at what sets it apart: "Premium Income." The Goldman Sachs S&P 500 Core Premium Income ETF paid a distribution yield of 8.3% over the last 12 months. How Emissions Jumped 45% on 100% Clean Power
Meta says it matched 100% of its electricity with clean and renewable energy for the sixth straight year. Direct Scope 1 emissions were just 33,555 tons, and market-based Scope 2 (purchased power) was 10,861 tons.

By our calculation, electricity use rose 34.9% to 24,849,122 megawatt-hours, and data centers used 24,523,035 of that. Power Limits Threaten the AI Plan Itself
The interconnection waiting lines and permitting delays that slowed clean energy also limit how fast new data centers can come online. Mark Zuckerberg spoke on the October 21, 2026[2] earnings call. He said Muse is “very compute-intensive to run”[2] and that “we have not launched it globally yet.”

Three Aristocrats in Two Accounts
Dividend Aristocrats are S&P 500 companies that have raised their dividends for at least 25 consecutive years. All three stocks below pay qualified dividends. In a taxable account, those dividends are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on income. Each position below is about $166,667.

This gap is smaller than it would be for BDCs or mortgage REITs, which pay ordinary income taxed at the full 24%. For Aristocrats, the case for a Roth comes down to three reasons.

The qualified-dividend rate grows with income. On top of it, the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) applies above $200,000 of income for single filers and $250,000 for joint filers.

Forrest Gump has nothing on Cameron Balser.
Doing his best impersonation of the fictional movie protagonist who developed a passion for running, Balser, a 35-year-old red-bearded and straggly-haired ultrarunner from Indiana, spent the past six weeks spreading messages of love, joy, and kindness on an epic quest to run across the U.S. in record time.
Averaging about 73.6 miles per day, the Kokomo, Indiana, runner left San Francisco at 5 a.m. PT on October 10 and ran across parts of 11 states before crossing the George Washington Bridge and entering New York City at 11:02 p.m. ET on Friday night. After running a few brisk miles through Manhattan, he eventually met up with his mom, stepdad, and two sisters and slowed to a walk on the final few blocks on the way to his finishing point.
His intent was to conclude his journey on the steps of New York City Hall, just as Pete Kostelnick did while setting his TransAmerica Run record of 42 days, 6 hours, and 30 minutes back in 2016.
The only trouble was that when Balser arrived in Lower Manhattan with a gaggle of two dozen or so friends, family members, and random followers, they found all of the gates to City Hall Park closed and locked. So instead, he walked to a point adjacent to City Hall and, like Gump mythically did in Monument Valley, Utah, he just stopped.
Balser officially ended his relentless push across the country at 11:45 p.m., which means he covered the 3,067-mile journey in a record-breaking 41 days, 16 hours, and 45 minutes—roughly 13 hours and 45 minutes faster than Kostelnick.

Missouri livestock farmers face environmental regulations. The CAFO debate should reflect that.
(Scott Olson/Getty Images)
A recent commentary in the Missouri Independent by Rural Crisis Center member Darvin Bentlage paints a misleading picture of Missouri’s livestock industry and the environmental safeguards that govern it.
Missouri’s livestock producers supply affordable, domestically produced protein while operating under state and federal environmental regulations designed to protect our natural resources. Those safeguards deserve to be part of the discussion.
The suggestion that Missouri livestock producers operate with virtually no environmental oversight overlooks important requirements already in place. Concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) are subject to extensive state and federal environmental requirements governing facility construction, manure storage, nutrient management, land application and water quality. Requirements vary by the size and type of operation.
Missouri’s CAFO policy is built to multiply pollution, not prevent it
These are not voluntary suggestions. They are enforceable regulations, and producers must comply or face penalties.
Start with the numbers. The commentary claims Missouri’s impaired waters list grew from 24 in 2002 to 549 today.But those figures do not provide a straightforward comparison of water quality over time. The state’s current list includes 24 impairments first identified in 2002, not a total of just 24 impairments that year.
The commentary also points to 215 listings added since 2020. An important part of the explanation is a change in how Missouri evaluates water quality. Missouri adopted numeric nutrient criteria for lakes in 2018, and the 2020 list was the first to be measured against those criteria.The new standards led to additional lakes being identified as impaired.
That is not evidence that livestock farms are driving a surge in pollution. Rather, as standards become more protective, more waters may be added to the impaired waters list. In fact, none of the 549 listings identifies a CAFO or livestock farm as its source.
The commentary also suggests that Missouri has no meaningful setback requirements. While Missouri does not require minimum spacing between separate CAFOs, other siting protections exist. Missouri regulations establish minimum separation distances. For example, CAFOs must be more than facilities generally must be at least 100 feet from human water supply lakes, losing streams or sinkholes. Larger operations are also subject to substantial buffer distances (in some cases, more than half a mile) from neighboring residences and public buildings, along with advance neighbor notification requirements. These safeguards exist for a reason: to protect neighboring landowners and natural resources while allowing responsible agricultural operations to continue.
Missouri’s approach to CAFO regulation recognizes that responsible facility siting involves far more than the distance between neighboring operations. Livestock operations must account for their surroundings, comply with established applicable engineering standards and meet environmental requirements.
Missouri’s regulatory framework includes setbacks from waterways and residences, though it does not establish minimum distances between separate CAFOs. Those existing safeguards are an important part of evaluating whether additional requirements are warranted.

Americans are shopping like there's no tomorrow.
A spate of high-profile technology outages that grounded planes, halted email access and slowed bank transactions have left many people worried about artificial intelligence-driven cyberattacks and the state of the U.S. energy grid.
Government officials have dismissed rumors and speculation circulating online that there could be a nefarious culprit for the series of malfunctions. Despite those assurances, consumers like Sabrina Cepeda are readying for a larger-scale technology blackout or other emergency event.
In recent days, the Houston resident has purchased propane and lighter fluid for cooking and heating equipment that can be used without electricity. The mother of three also replenished her backup stockpiles of non-perishable foods, hygiene products and allergy medicine in the event that her family is homebound for several days.
"I have a way to keep my family fed, clean, hydrated, warm and safe," said Cepeda, 39. "You want to have these things and not need them, rather than need them and not have them."
The doomsday economy is catching a bid. Wall Street and retailers are taking note.
Emergency prep buying
At least half a dozen major technology outages took place in the U.S. between Nov. 12 and Nov. 17. In that time frame, spending at brands specializing in emergency products spiked about 400% compared with the same period a year prior, according to card data analyzed exclusively for CNBC by Consumer Edge.

In addition, corporate customers who keep the Vista, California-based company's supplies in their offices in case of emergency have called in to order more.

As a result, Ready America asked its suppliers to scale up production. A powerful stride depends on having a strong core. It’s basically the glue that holds your running form together and will make every mile more efficient, helping you hit faster speeds.
But between fitting in runs, setting aside time for recovery, fueling, and living life outside of running shoes, it’s hard to know if you’re dedicating enough time to strengthening this key muscle group. So when your calendar is already packed, what’s the minimum number of core workouts you need to do to reap the benefits?
We asked experts for that magic minimum number, so you can boost your performance without carving a ton of time out of your busy schedule.
The Minimum Amount of Core Work Runners Need
Simply put, every runner should aim to get at least two 10- to 15-minute core sessions done per week, says Yusuf Jeffers, NYC-based strength and run coach, Hyrox race director, and Nike Well Collective trainer. This is an adequate number to support your running form, build more strength and power, and improve overall running efficiency.
However, several factors can adjust this number, including your running goals and the season you’re in, says Holly Dickinson, UESCA-certified run coach, NSCA-certified strength and conditioning coach, and owner of StrideHer run coaching. For example, if building strength is your offseason goal and you’re not running as much mileage as you would during race training, you might increase the minimum amount of core work you do to three or four sessions per week. During a racing season, though, you might stick to two sessions per week.
As for the exercises you need, you can skip moves like crunches, which can stress your back and neck muscles and isolate just a few ab muscles (namely, the rectus abdominis or those six-pack abs) and instead, go for moves like planks, bird dogs, Copenhagen side planks, and glute bridges. These moves help with spinal and pelvic stability and core muscular endurance, and mimic running form—plus, they work 360 degrees of your core.
Jeffers recommends spending at least 30 seconds on each move, completing your core work in a circuit-style fashion (which means completing each move back-to-back with minimal rest in between) and repeating the circuit for at least two sets.
If you strength train regularly, you probably don’t have to do any additional core workouts because many programs often require you to brace your midsection and keep your spine neutral in order to do the exercise properly, Jeffers adds, which is basically like built-in core work. Think of weighted back squats, deadlifts, and bench presses, for example. You need to engage your core to maintain a stable spine through all of these exercises.
Why Runners Need Regular Core Work
Many people tend to think of the core as just ab muscles, but your core is literally everything that’s not your arms and legs, says Jeffers. That’s essentially everything from your abdominal muscles to your glutes, pelvic floor, and back. All of these muscles work together to keep you stable on your runs and prevent form breakdown.
